terms.definition: The body's process of keeping internal conditions (like temperature) stable and balanced, even when the outside environment changes.
terms.function: Coordinates sensing and response systems across the body so that once a corrective response brings a condition back to its set point, the signal stops and balance is restored.
terms.whereItIs: Not a single structure — an ongoing, body-wide balancing act coordinated by the nervous and endocrine systems.
terms.whyItMatters: Homeostasis is why your body can keep working properly across a huge range of outside conditions, from a freezing morning to a sweaty afternoon run.

terms.definition: A small structure at the base of the brain that senses body temperature and sends signals to trigger cooling or warming responses.
terms.function: Constantly compares blood temperature and nerve signals from the skin against the body's set point (about 37°C / 98.6°F) and fires off the matching cooling or warming response.
terms.whereItIs: Deep in the brain, near its base — exposed on a mid-skull cross-section of the head.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the body's thermostat — without it constantly checking and adjusting, temperature would simply drift with the outside environment.

terms.definition: The widening of blood vessels near the skin's surface, which lets more warm blood flow close to the skin so heat can escape into the air.
terms.function: Increases blood flow near the skin surface so heat can radiate and convect away from the body faster, working alongside sweating to cool the body down.
terms.whereItIs: In the small blood vessels just under the skin, most visible where skin flushes red during exercise or heat.
terms.whyItMatters: It's one half of the body's cooling response — without it, heat would stay trapped closer to the body's core.

terms.definition: The narrowing of blood vessels near the skin's surface, which reduces blood flow there and helps keep body heat locked in the core.
terms.function: Redirects warm blood away from the skin surface and deeper into the body's core, reducing how much heat is lost to cold surroundings.
terms.whereItIs: In the small blood vessels just under the skin, most noticeable as pale skin in cold weather.
terms.whyItMatters: It's one half of the body's warming response, working alongside shivering to protect core temperature when it's cold.

terms.definition: A control system where a change triggers a response that pushes things back toward the original, steady state — like a thermostat turning off the heater once a room reaches the target temperature.
terms.function: Keeps a condition like body temperature within a narrow, safe range by continuously sensing deviation and triggering a corrective response that cancels it out.
terms.whereItIs: Not a physical structure — a pattern of cause and effect running through the nervous system, blood vessels, sweat glands, and muscles together.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the underlying mechanism that makes temperature regulation (and many other body processes) self-correcting instead of spiraling out of control.

terms.definition: The overall process of controlling and maintaining a stable internal body temperature.
terms.function: Combines sensing (by the hypothalamus) with cooling responses (sweating, vasodilation) and warming responses (shivering, vasoconstriction) to hold core temperature near its set point.
terms.whereItIs: A whole-body process coordinated by the hypothalamus, carried out by the skin, blood vessels, sweat glands, and muscles.
terms.whyItMatters: It's the umbrella term for everything this component covers — the reason your body can stay safe in both a heat wave and a snowstorm.
